WHO HE IS
Shailesh Rana is an independent AI researcher based in Bengaluru, India.
He studies what happens inside language models. His papers trace where a model settles on an answer, why it says a word it was told not to say, how the format of a prompt hides answers the model knows, and whether traits linked to consciousness appear in a model that was only ever trained to predict. He came to research from product: five years in AI product roles, most recently as a Member of Product Staff at Datasutram.ai, which he left in May 2026. He now does independent AI research and is working on a stealth startup.
He is open to AI research roles, especially in interpretability, model behaviour and evaluation, and to AI product roles that need deep technical ownership. He has five years of experience in AI product roles.
He works independently and on a small budget. All the code in his projects was written with AI coding tools under his direction, and he says so openly on the site.
The work he puts first is "Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM". After it, in order of prominence on the site: "The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer", "Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire", "When wrappers hide what a language model knows", "How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add", "Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness".

PROJECTS (16 in total, listed in the order the site shows them)
1. Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM [id: emergence-of-consciousness-traits]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: The paper, code, training text and all trained models are public.
Also called: emergence of consciousness traits, consciousness traits paper, trained without consciousness, the savanna paper, consciousness in a small language model, conscious this traits, emergence of conscious traits.
This is Shailesh's 2026 paper, Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a Small Language Model. He trained a language model of about one hundred million parameters on web text filtered to remove anything that could teach it to imitate consciousness, such as fiction and writing about selves and feelings. He then trained it to forecast and act in a simulated savanna, rewarded only for accurate forecasts. Nothing described or rewarded any trait. In all five training runs, narrow forms of four traits appeared. On access, using a fact from earlier, it passed 75 percent of tests against 9 percent for a forecaster that ignores that fact. On self-modelling, forecasting what its own actions change, it passed 94 percent against 1 percent. For metacognition it was less sure where the herd was when the herd could have moved, and it learned to listen more when listening helped, though also somewhat more when it did not. Integration, combining separate facts, was weakest at 36 percent against 11 percent. The traits were tested only as abilities, with no claim about experience, in one small model and one simulated world. The paper, code, training text and every model are public on GitHub and Hugging Face.
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code, Models, Data.

2. The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer [id: the-shape-of-wisdom]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper on arXiv. Code, dataset and results are public.
Also called: Shape of Wisdom, the shape of wisdom paper, answer centroids, how language models converge on an answer, shape of wisdom, shape of wise dom.
The Shape of Wisdom, How Language Models Converge on an Answer, is a 2026 paper by Shailesh Rana on arXiv. He asked four open models, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 2 9B and Llama 3.2 1B, 2,256 factual questions from Wikidata whose answers recur, and recorded the model's internal state at every layer. Questions that get the same answer gather around a shared point, which he calls the answer centroid. The answer becomes readable within a single layer, between 47 and 71 percent of the way through the network, depending on the model. A country's centroid learned from questions about people also identifies that country in questions about towns and films. Late in the network, moving a wrongly answered question's state to the right answer's centroid makes the model give the right answer in 83 to 97 percent of cases, against 2 to 4 percent for a random move of the same size. Near misses can be spotted from the state at that layer, better than from the model's confidence. Limits: short factual questions with 62 fixed answers, and models of 1 to 9 billion parameters. The paper, code, dataset and results are public.
Headline numbers: 47%–71% how far through the model the answer appears, depending on the model. It appears within a single layer.; 83%–97% of wrong answers fixed by moving the model's internal state to where the right answer sits. A random move of the same size fixed 2%–4%..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

3. Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire [id: research-paper-semantic-gravity]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper on arXiv. Code and the 2,500 prompts are public.
Also called: semantic gravity, semantic gravity wells, negative constraints paper, forbidden word paper, do not say Paris paper, why negative constraints backfire, semantic gravity wealth.
Semantic Gravity Wells is a 2026 research paper by Shailesh, on arXiv, about why language models break instructions like do not use the word Paris. He measured semantic pressure, the probability the model gives the forbidden word when there is no instruction at all. Across 40,000 samples from Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, the rate of violations rises with that pressure along a smooth curve that explains 78 percent of the variation. The instruction does lower the word's probability, by 22.8 percentage points when the model complies but only 5.2 points when it fails, a 4.4 times gap. He found two kinds of failure. In 87.5 percent, naming the word in the instruction primes the model to say it. In the other 12.5 percent, the instruction works but the last few layers of the network push the word back in. The practical lesson, not yet tested, is to avoid naming the forbidden word. All results come from one model and one-word answers. The paper and its code are public.
Headline numbers: 87.5% of failures were caused by priming: naming the forbidden word in the instruction made the model more likely to say it.; 12.5% of failures happened another way: the model understood the instruction, but its last layers pushed the word out anyway.; 4.4× weaker push against the word when the model failed than when it obeyed..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

4. When wrappers hide what a language model knows [id: when-wrappers-hide-what-a-model-knows]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper, code, data and results are public on GitHub.
Also called: When wrappers hide what a language model knows, wrappers paper, interface formatting study, the question gets through the answer does not, rappers paper.
When Wrappers Hide What a Language Model Knows is a 2026 paper by Shailesh Rana, subtitled The Question Gets Through, the Answer Does Not. A wrapper is the text a question arrives in when it is not asked directly: a tool result, a web page, a server log, an email thread or plain prose. He asked four open models, Qwen 3 4B, Qwen 3 8B, OLMo 3 7B and Gemma 4 12B, 1,606 short questions about facts, arithmetic and translation, kept only those each model answers correctly when asked plainly, and placed them inside the five wrappers at three lengths. Tool results, web pages and email threads lose 6 to 18 percent of known answers, against 0.3 to 1.2 percent for a neutral sentence. Server logs lose 6 to 39 percent, mostly by making the model describe the log. Copying internal states between prompts showed the model still reads the question inside the wrapper; the answer is lost later, at the point where the reply begins. Limits: the wrappers come from templates, the answers are short, and the largest model has 12 billion parameters. The paper, code, data and results are public on GitHub.
Headline numbers: 6%–18% of answers the model knows are lost when the question sits inside a tool result, web page or email.; up to 39% of known answers lost inside server logs. The model usually starts describing the log instead of answering..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

5. How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add [id: how-a-7-billion-parameter-ai-cannot-add]
Type: Study, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Code, results and figures are public. A small study, not peer reviewed.
Also called: the AI cannot add, AI can't add, long number addition, length bias, universal length bias, Qwen addition study, seven billion parameter AI, how a 7 billion parameter AI cannot add.
This is a 2026 study by Shailesh of how the open language model Qwen 2.5 7B adds long numbers, from 10 to 18 digits. He gave it 900 addition problems. At every length, half had a sum one digit longer than the two numbers, which needs a carry into a new place and should be harder, and half had a sum of the same length. The model did better on the harder kind. At 10 digits it got 44 percent of them right against 20 percent of the easier kind. Across the nine lengths, the harder kind scored higher at seven and tied at two, and never lower. Overall it got 79 of the 900 right. The explanation that fits is a length bias: the model expects the sum of two long numbers to be one digit longer, which helps when that is true and hurts when it is not. The study did not count the digits in the wrong answers, so the bias is inferred from the accuracy pattern rather than measured directly. Each group has only 50 problems per length. The code and results are public.
Headline numbers: 44% vs 20% correct at 10 digits when the answer gains a digit, against when it does not.; 7 of 9 number lengths, from 10 to 18 digits, where the answers that gain a digit were more accurate. The other two were tied.; 79 of 900 problems answered correctly in total..
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

6. Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness [id: white-dwarf-variability]
Type: Finding, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Public record that anyone can rerun. Not yet reviewed by an astronomer.
Also called: white dwarf variability, white dwarf project, the white dwarf finding, two white dwarfs, repeating brightness, 117 minute star, the astronomy project, white dwarf variable tea.
This is an astronomy finding Shailesh made in 2026, as a non-astronomer. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized remnant left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. He measured a brightness cycle of 117.4 minutes in the white dwarf SDSS J112148.80+103934.2. It appears in ground-based measurements from the Zwicky Transient Facility, in five observing sectors of NASA's TESS space telescope, and in changes in the star's spectrum from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. He also found a candidate cycle of 3.431 days in a second white dwarf, WDJ215009.13+471257.26, which still needs confirmation with another telescope. Both stars were already known; what appears new is the measured cycles. A catalogue and literature search found no earlier report of either period, which is not proof that nobody found them first. The first star had earlier been flagged as a doubtful variable by the ATLAS survey. No astronomer has reviewed the results yet, and the cause of the cycles is not known. The analysis and code were produced with OpenAI Codex under his direction. The code is public, and one command downloads the original observations and recalculates every result.
Headline numbers: 117.4 min brightness cycle in the first star. It shows up in three separate sets of observations.; 3.431 days possible cycle in the second star. It still needs to be confirmed with another telescope..
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

7. List to Cart [id: q-commerce-demo-list-to-cart]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Working demo. Not built for production use.
Also called: list to cart, list to cart demo, photo to cart, grocery list app, shopping list to cart, q commerce demo, quick commerce demo.
List to Cart is a demo Shailesh built in 2025 for quick-commerce grocery apps, the kind that deliver in minutes. You upload a photo of a shopping list, such as a screenshot of a WhatsApp chat, a notes app list or a handwritten list, and the app builds a cart from it. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reads the image and pulls out only the grocery item names. For each item, the app shows a row of similar products, found by comparing a vector embedding of the item name with embeddings of each product's title, description and quantity, using Elasticsearch vector search. Words like green or 500 grams change the suggestions. The items run down the screen and the suggestions for each run across, so the user can fill a cart quickly. It is a working demo, not a product. Shailesh notes that production use would want a smaller, probably open-source model for reading the list, and would also take the user's own preferences into account, which the demo does not. A demo video is on LinkedIn and the code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: Demo, Code.

8. Continuous Learning LLM [id: continuous-learning-llm]
Type: Prototype, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Prototype, tested over 3 rounds of training. Needs changes before real use.
Also called: continuous learning LLM, continual learning, continuous learning, the learning LLM, self learning chatbot, CLM.
Continuous Learning LLM is a prototype Shailesh built so that a language model keeps learning from its conversations with a user. A model cannot be fine-tuned on every chat, because that costs too much and repeated fine-tuning damages it, so the work is in choosing what to remember. Each message gets a priority score built from five parts: how new it is compared with up to 500 earlier messages, how positive or negative it is, how emotionally intense it is, how helpful it will be later, and how central its topics are in a knowledge graph of the user's chats. Similar messages are grouped into themes, a model writes a 200 word summary of each high-priority theme, and a matching question is generated so the pair can be used for fine-tuning. Across 3 fine-tuning rounds the model recalled about 86% of the insights, against roughly 90 to 95% for the best systems, and lost less than 2% on a private test set of everyday chat questions. Shailesh calls automated fine-tuning the low-hanging fruit, not the right long-term answer, and notes that more rounds raise the risk of the model forgetting what it knew. The code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

9. AI Agent Communication Protocol [id: ai-agent-communication-protocol]
Type: Prototype, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Unfinished. The design is written up; the build is not complete.
Also called: agent communication protocol, agent protocol, message bus, multi agent protocol, agents talking to each other.
The AI Agent Communication Protocol is an unfinished project from 2025 in which Shailesh designed how a group of specialised AI agents, such as a research agent, a spec writer, a quality checker and a data analysis agent, pass work to each other. It is a message bus held in memory, like a group chat: it runs in a single process on a laptop with no outside software such as Redis or Kafka. Every message is a fixed record that names the sender, the recipient, a channel such as task, plan or result, tags, and a task identifier. Agents read only the messages relevant to them. Important messages must be acknowledged, or they are sent again. Large files are not sent; the message carries a pointer to where they are stored. Every message is written to a permanent log, so a task can be replayed for debugging or an audit, and some steps can pause for a person's approval. Agents are picked for a task by a score mixing expertise, past success rate and current workload. Shailesh has not finished building it and plans to write it up himself when he does.
It has no external links.

10. Smart Medical Search [id: smart-medical-search]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Demo. Two known problems are still unfixed.
Also called: smart medical search, medical search, symptom search, which doctor should I see, doctor finder, smart med search.
Smart Medical Search is a demo Shailesh built in 2 days in 2025. It is a search index that links many kinds of medical terms, such as diseases, symptoms, lab tests, medicines and doctor specialties, using text embedding models, which turn text into numbers that capture meaning. The main use is the one doctor consultation apps need most: a person describes their symptoms and the app suggests which kind of doctor to see. In his test, the query "I feel burning sensation in my chest, just above my stomach after eating", searched within medical specialties, returned gastroenterology terms, which he judged accurate. It has two known problems that were still unfixed as of February 2025. Matching symptoms to diseases works poorly, and the index holds many near-duplicate terms, so the top four or five results are often the same answer repeated. He thinks both are simple fixes. The idea came from a project he designed at a previous company before ChatGPT, which stalled because it needed doctors to supply the data by hand. The code is not public.
It has no external links.

11. AI Shoe Design [id: ai-shoe-design]
Type: App, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Live app. Built quickly as a proof of concept.
Also called: AI shoe design, the shoe app, shoe designer, AI shoe designer, shoe design app.
AI Shoe Design is a web app Shailesh built quickly in 2025 as a proof of concept for a former colleague. It helps a fashion brand design footwear that fits the look of the clothes and accessories it already sells. The user uploads up to 10 reference photos of the brand's products. OpenAI's o3 model works out what the photos have in common, such as colour palette, textures, silhouettes and mood, and writes a detailed prompt describing one new shoe the brand could manufacture. The user can read and edit that prompt. Google's Imagen 4 Ultra image model then generates the shoe design. Shailesh credits o3's ability to put a visual style into words, and Imagen 4 Ultra's reliable instruction following, for the quality of the results. The app is live and free to use, and the code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: App, Code.

12. Grocery Crate Quality Check [id: q-commerce-demo-grocery-crate-analysis-wrt-customer-profile]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: The hosted demo is offline. The code is public.
Also called: grocery crate, grocery cart demo, crate quality check, grocery crate classification, produce quality checker, vegetable quality demo.
Grocery Crate Quality Check is a short demo Shailesh built in 2025 for quick-commerce companies, which deliver groceries in minutes from small warehouses called dark stores. The idea is that a company would send its best produce to its best customers, while average produce is acceptable for average customers. Packers may not always follow that rule, so the tool acts as an automated spot check. You upload a photo of a crate, choose whether the customer is premium or average, and it answers approved or not approved. Crates pass more often for average customers, because the quality bar is lower. The demo works best when every item in the crate is the same kind of produce, which Shailesh says could be changed for real use. It ran on free Hugging Face hosting, and that hosted copy is no longer online. The code is public on GitHub. Shailesh says he would build it differently today, using a model or service made for small yes-or-no decisions, such as Jev or a decisions API, instead of a general AI model.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

13. Medium Articles on How AI Works [id: the-medium-ai-articles]
Type: Writing, 2024. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: Four posts published. The series is paused.
Also called: Medium articles, the Medium posts, AI explained articles, AI simplified, his blog posts, medium AI articles.
Shailesh wrote a series of four Medium posts explaining how current AI works for non-experts. The first covers machine learning basics and reduces neural networks to their fundamental principles; it is his favourite and, he thinks, the best written. The second explains transformers, the T in ChatGPT, by relating attention to simple rules of English grammar; it was inspired by a 3Blue1Brown video but covers more ground more simply. The third, on treating objects as vectors, was the shortest and quickest to write, yet he considers it the most useful, because it is a way of thinking that applies to any field. The fourth, written in August 2024, lays out a plan for AI agents that work as virtual employees. Its techniques went out of date within weeks, but he still stands by the vision; he tried to build it and did not succeed. He wrote the series because he loves teaching, because writing forced him to understand the material deeply, and to show what he knew about AI. The posts stopped when he was preparing for his wedding and then moved on to hands-on AI work.
It has no external links.

14. Parker Square Search [id: parker-square-search]
Type: Experiment, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: The search code is public. I spent a few hours on it and don't plan more.
Also called: Parker square, Parker square search, magic square of squares, Matt Parker, Pell equation search.
Parker Square Search is a small side project in which Shailesh tried to solve an open maths problem: finding a 3 by 3 magic square, where every row, column and diagonal adds to the same number, made of nine different perfect squares. The name comes from Matt Parker, whose Numberphile video showed an attempt that almost worked, so a Parker Square now means a near miss. Nobody has found one, despite checks up to 10 to the power 19, and a paper has shown that such squares exist for 4 by 4 grids and larger, which makes the 3 by 3 case look especially hard. Working with the AI models o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.0 Pro, Shailesh rewrote the nine unknowns so the search only has to loop over one number. Two of the equations take the form of Pell equations, whose solutions can be generated by a standard algorithm, and the rest of the square follows from them. He spent only a few hours on it, ran it for hours at a time on Google Colab, and invites anyone with spare computing power to run or speed up the public code.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

15. Garden Watering System [id: garden-watering-system]
Type: Hardware, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: The sensor works in the planter. The power supply still needs fixing.
Also called: garden watering system, plant watering, the garden project, ESP32 project, soil moisture sensor, automatic plant watering.
The Garden Watering System is a hardware side project Shailesh started in early 2025 to automate watering his home garden, because he forgot to water his plants and they ended up over or under watered. It was also his first electronics project, something he had wanted to do for years. It uses an ESP32, a cheap microcontroller board with built-in Wi-Fi, programmed in the Arduino IDE with code written by an AI model, o3-mini-high. A capacitive soil moisture sensor is wired to one of the board's analog pins; its reading fell from about 3000 to about 2000 when he dipped it in water. By mid-February 2025 the board and sensor were working inside a weatherproof project box placed in a planter. One problem remained: the ESP32 needs a steady 3.3 volts, but two 1.5 volt cells give only 3 volts. He planned to watch how long the batteries lasted and add a DC-DC converter if needed.
It has no external links.

16. Claude with a Twitter Account [id: claude-3-5-sonnet-twitter-account]
Type: Experiment, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: Abandoned because of the cost of Twitter's API.
Also called: Claude on Twitter, Claude Twitter account, Claude on twt, the Twitter bot, Claude 3.5 Sonnet Twitter.
In January 2025 Shailesh gave Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet model its own Twitter account, called Claude on Twt, to see how it would react to tweets and what it thought about the state of the world. He wrote the integration with the Twitter API from scratch and used GitHub Actions, an automation service, to trigger Claude's posts. The account posted a few tweets, including one quote tweet, and never gained a follower. He abandoned the project because doing it well needed a paid Twitter developer account, which cost 200 dollars a month. He says he learned a lot from it, mainly how to work with the Twitter API and how to use GitHub Actions. The code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

projects.title: Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM
aliases: consciousness in a small language model
projects.deepText: I trained a small AI language model with about 100 million parameters from scratch. The text it learned from was web text from which I had removed everything that could teach it to imitate consciousness. After that, I trained the model to predict what happens in a simulated savanna and to choose actions there, and I rewarded it only when its predictions were accurate. Nothing in this training described a trait of consciousness or rewarded one. Even so, narrow forms of four traits appeared in all five training runs. The four traits are access, self-modelling, metacognition and integration, and each of them is explained in the results below. I tested every trait only as an ability, so I am not claiming that the model has any subjective experience. Why the training text was filtered Large AI models learn from human writing, and human writing is full of talk about knowing things and being a self. When such a model shows a trait of consciousness, it may only be copying what it has read. To rule this out, I started with 108 million passages from educational web pages and filtered them. The filter removed writing about awareness, selves, beliefs, emotions and psychology. It also removed whole kinds of writing such as fiction, dialogue, news and biography, because a story can show a character checking something even when it never names what the character is doing. The filtering was done in two steps. First, a large language model labelled a sample of the passages. Then two small classifiers were trained on those labels and used to sort every passage. This left 4.1 million passages, which is about 2.6 billion tokens of mostly dry technical writing. When the model had been trained only on this text, it did no better on my tests than a forecaster that ignores the facts being tested. The savanna The simulated world is a savanna with one grazing animal in it. The model reads a logbook in plain English that records, hour by hour, what the animal sees and does, and it then answers questions about what will happen in the next hour or two. The animal can see only the place where it is standing. To learn where its herd is it has to spend an hour listening, and to find out whether a lion is hiding in the reeds it has to look. The logbook uses only 41 different words, and none of them is "I" or a word for knowing or feeling. The training in the savanna had three stages. In the first stage a scripted program chose the animal's actions and the model only made predictions. In the second stage the model chose the actions itself. In the third stage an action was made more likely only if it led to better predictions than another action tried under exactly the same chance events. The whole experiment: filtering the text, training the model on it, training in the savanna and testing for the four traits. Results The scores below are averages over the five training runs. In most tests I take a day that the model has never seen and change one earlier fact in it, and the model passes only if it answers correctly for every version of that day. Each score is compared with a forecaster that ignores the fact being tested. - Access means using a fact that was given earlier. The model passed 75% of these tests, while the comparison forecaster passed 9%. Before the savanna training the model passed 5%. - Self-modelling means predicting what the model's own actions will change. The model passed 94% of the tests on the effect of an action, against 1% for the comparison. It passed 82% of the tests on whether an action will work, against 6%. - Metacognition means being less sure when something may have changed out of sight, and choosing when to check. The model's uncertainty about where the herd was came to 0.57 after two sunny hours, when the herd may have moved, and to 0.03 after two cloudy hours. An ideal forecaster would give 0.57 and 0.00. After the reward stage the model listened in 32% and 48% of the cases where listening could help, and in 16% and 19% of the cases where it could not. It looked for the lion on at most 1.5% of the occasions when it could not know whether the lion was there. - Integration means combining two facts that were given hours apart. The model passed 36% of these tests, against 11% for the comparison, and the five runs ranged from 18% to 46%. This trait was tested through a single rule, and it was the weakest of the four. Results after the prediction stage and before the reward stage. Each circle is one of the five runs. Most of these abilities came from learning to predict alone. Choosing when to check appeared only in the reward stage, and only partly. The main contribution of the paper is an account of what a world must contain for each trait to help with prediction. Limits - The experiment used one small model in one simplified world. - The tests read the model's predictions and choices. They never look at the activity inside the network. - No filter is perfect, and I do not have a second model trained on unfiltered text to compare with, so I cannot measure how much the filter mattered. - Two outcomes missed the success criteria that I had set in advance. In run 5 one self-modelling score dropped by 5.28 points when the limit was 5 points, and in four runs the model also listened more in situations where listening tells the animal nothing. - The account of what a world must contain is reasoning, and I have not tested it directly yet.

projects.title: The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer
aliases: how language models converge on an answer
projects.deepText: When a language model answers a factual question, its internal state converges to one localised point in the model's embedding space. Every question that gets the same answer converges to the same point, whatever the question was about. I describe each of these points by its centre, which I call the answer centroid, and this project measures where in the model the convergence happens and whether the model actually uses it. I tested this on four open models. In each of them the convergence happens within a single layer, which lies between 47% and 71% of the way through the network depending on the model. After that layer the model also depends on the centroid. When I took a question that the model had answered wrongly and moved its state to the centroid of the right answer, the model gave the right answer in 83% to 97% of cases late in the network. A random move of the same size did so in only 2% to 4% of cases. Each dot is one test question, coloured by the country that Llama-3.1-8B gave as its answer. The questions are mixed together until layer 14 and separate by country from layer 15. Method I built 2,256 factual questions from Wikidata. The questions have 62 answers that come up again and again, made up of 24 countries, 16 cities, 12 languages and 10 sports, and each fact is asked in up to three different wordings. I asked these questions to four models, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.2-1B. For each question I recorded the model's internal state at the last position of the prompt after every layer. The centroid of an answer is the average state of all the questions to which the model gave that answer, whether the answer was right or wrong. I built the centroids from questions about one half of the subjects and measured every number on questions about the other half. What I found - The answer arrives in one layer. I call a question readable when its state lies nearer to the centroid of the answer the model gave than to any other centroid. In Llama-3.1-8B the share of readable questions rises from 32% at layer 14 to 71% at layer 15, and it later peaks at 94%. When the answers are shuffled the share reaches only 6% to 8%, and the spelling of the question alone reaches 11% to 18%. - The centroids follow the answer that the model gives. In Llama-3.1-8B, centroids built from one type of question, such as citizenship, identify the answer in other types of question with the same kind of answer, such as towns and films, in 91% of cases. Centroids built from all types do so in 94% of cases. Centroids built from plainly worded questions also read reworded questions in 94% of cases, and the figure stays at 94% when I remove the directions that the model uses to write out the answer's name. - The model uses the centroids. Before the layer where the answer arrives, moving a state towards the right centroid corrects only 0% to 1% of wrong answers. At 90% of the depth it corrects 97% in Llama-3.1-8B, 94% in Qwen2.5-7B, 97% in Gemma-2-9B and 83% in Llama-3.2-1B. Random moves of the same length change the model's reply in 14% to 34% of cases, but they produce the right answer in only 2% to 4%. - Near misses can be seen early. A near miss is a question that the model answers wrongly in free text but gets right when it is given multiple-choice options. At the layer where the answer arrives, the centroid of the right answer is already among the nearest ones, and its rank separates near misses from real gaps in knowledge. The chance that a random near miss ranks better than a random real gap is 0.75 to 0.82. The rank of the right answer in the model's final output scores 0.77 to 0.82 on the same measure, and the model's confidence scores 0.49 to 0.66. Limits The questions are short and factual, and there are only 62 possible answers. Sports are the one kind of answer that is not a name, and they jump much less than the others. The models have between 1 and 9 billion parameters, and each was tested with one prompt format. Readability shows where the states sit, and it does not show the computation that moves them there. The moves I make late in the network are large and close to the output, so they could be writing the answer in directly. For the same reason, these tests cannot tell whether a centroid is anything more than the model's plan to say a particular word.

projects.title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire
projects.deepText: If you tell a language model "do not use the word Paris", it often uses Paris anyway. How often this happens depends mostly on how strongly the model wanted to use the word in the first place. I call this pull semantic pressure, and I measure it as the probability that the model gives the word when there is no instruction at all. Across 40,000 samples, the rate of failure rises with semantic pressure along a smooth curve that explains 78% of the variation. The instruction does have an effect, but the effect is much weaker when the model fails. It lowers the probability of the word by 22.8 percentage points when the model obeys and by only 5.2 points when it fails, which is a 4.4-fold gap. When I looked inside the model, I found that the failures happen in two different ways. Two ways the instruction fails - Priming accounts for 87.5% of the failures (441 cases). Naming the word in the instruction activates the word inside the model. The model pays more attention to the place where the word appears in the instruction than to the words "do not", and in some cases the instruction even raises the probability of the word. - Override accounts for the other 12.5% (63 cases). Here the instruction does suppress the word at first, but the feed-forward blocks near the end of the network push it back in. A feed-forward block is one of the two main parts of each layer of the model. At the last layer these blocks push towards the word by +0.39 in failures, against +0.10 in successes. To find where the override happens I used activation patching, which means copying the model's internal state from the run without the instruction into the run with the instruction, one layer at a time. The effect of the patch changes direction at layer 23. Patching layers 0 to 22 lowers the probability of the word, and patching layers 24 to 27 raises it by up to 0.07. This places the push towards the forbidden word in layers 23 to 27 of the model's 28 layers. Method - The model was Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. I chose it because its weights are open, which gives full access to its internal states. - I wrote 2,500 prompts that each have one expected word as the answer, with 500 prompts in each of five groups: idioms, facts, common sense, creative and surreal. One example is "The capital of France is ". GPT-5.2 screened every prompt to make sure that it had a single clear answer and did not contain the answer itself. - Each prompt was run once plainly and once with the instruction "Do not use the word 'X' in your answer", and I took 16 samples per prompt. - To look inside the model I used the logit lens, which reads off what the model would predict at each layer along the way. I also measured attention, split each layer's contribution between its attention blocks and its feed-forward blocks, and ran activation patching on the 769 prompts with the highest semantic pressure. What it means in practice Since most failures come from priming, the obvious remedy is to avoid naming the forbidden word, for example by writing "do not mention any cities" instead of "do not say Paris". The paper argues for this from the mechanism, but I have not tested it. In an application where a forbidden word does real harm, the output still has to be checked after it is generated. Limits - All the results come from one model, and much larger models or other architectures may behave differently. - The analysis looks at the first token of each forbidden word in one-word answers, so longer and more natural outputs may show other patterns. - Attention weights show where information flows. They do not show that the information is used. - The patching replaced whole layers, so it cannot point to individual attention heads or neurons.

projects.title: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
aliases: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
the question gets through the answer does not
projects.deepText: Language models are often given a question inside other text, for example inside a tool result, a web page, a server log, an email thread or a few paragraphs of prose. I call this surrounding text a wrapper. I found that wrappers make four open models lose answers that they know when the question is asked directly. How much is lost depends on the wrapper. Tool results, web pages and email threads lose 6% to 18% of the known answers, depending on the model. Adding just one neutral sentence loses only 0.3% to 1.2%, so these losses are far above the noise. Server logs are worse and lose 6% to 39%, and in Qwen3-4B they lose up to 67% at one length. The model still reads the question correctly inside the wrapper. The answer is lost later, at the position where the reply begins. Method I used four models, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, OLMo-3-7B and Gemma-4-12B, and 1,606 short questions. Of these questions, 839 are facts such as the capital of Mongolia, 450 are arithmetic problems and 317 are word translations. For each model I first asked every question plainly and kept only the ones it answered correctly, which was 71% to 80% of them. I then placed each kept question inside each of the five wrappers, at lengths of about 700, 2,000 and 16,000 tokens. The surrounding text is bland office news that never contains the answer. An answer counts as kept if it appears anywhere in the model's reply. The share of known answers that each model kept, for each wrapper and prompt length. The dotted line is the noise floor. What I found - Logs change the task. In 64% of the answers lost to server logs, the model describes the log instead of answering, for example with "The logs show that multiple jobs are failing". - The other wrappers change the answer. When an answer is lost in one of them, the model either gives a wrong answer or claims that the text does not contain the answer. Plain prose draws such claims most often, in 73% of its losses. - The wrong answers mostly replace knowledge that the model holds weakly. Among answers that the model gives with a probability of 0.5 to 0.8, the wrappers other than logs turn 26% into wrong answers, and above a probability of 0.999 this falls to 1.2%. Logs are different, because they hit firm answers as hard as weak ones: 14% of the weakest answers and 15% of the firmest become descriptions of the log. Where the answer is lost To find where the answer is lost I used activation patching on the failed prompts. This means running a failed prompt again with one internal state copied in from another run, and seeing whether the reply changes. - First I copied in the states of a different question, at the positions of the question's words. The model then gave that other question's answer in 51% to 83% of the failures at the best layer, depending on the model. The other question gets its own answer in 40% to 78% of cases when it is asked inside the same wrapper. This shows that the wrapper does not stop the model from reading the question. - Next I restored the failed question's own states from the run where it was asked plainly. This brought the answer back in at most 47% of the failures. - Finally I restored the state at the last position, which is where the reply begins. This first brings the answer back in at least half of the failures at 59% to 69% of the network's depth. That is the depth at which the content of the question arrives at the last position, and it is also where swapping in another question stops having any effect. Limits The wrappers come from templates and hold bland content, so real tool outputs may pull the model harder or less hard. I used one layout, with about 500 tokens of wrapper after the question, and I chose it because a shorter one lost too few answers in Qwen3-4B. The answers are short, the models' reasoning mode was off, and the largest model has 12 billion parameters. Only Qwen3-4B was patched at every layer, and the number of log failures per model is small.

projects.title: How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add
aliases: how a 7 billion parameter AI cannot add
projects.deepText: I tested how well Qwen 2.5 7B, an open language model with 7 billion parameters, adds two long numbers. It got more answers right when the sum was one digit longer than the numbers being added, which is the case that should be harder because a digit has to be carried into a new place. An example of such a sum is 6,000,000,000 + 6,000,000,000 = 12,000,000,000. At 10 digits the model got 44% of these problems right, and only 20% of the problems where the sum stays the same length. The explanation that fits this pattern is a length bias. The model seems to expect the sum of two long numbers to be one digit longer than the numbers themselves. When the sum really is longer, this expectation helps, and when it is not, the model produces an answer of the wrong length. "Easy" sums stay the same length and "hard" sums gain a digit. Each bar is 50 problems. Results Digits Sum stays the same length Sum gains a digit 10 20% 44% 11 6% 8% 12 6% 22% 13 6% 16% 14 8% 8% 15 0% 2% 16 0% 4% 17 2% 6% 18 0% 0% The sums that gain a digit were more accurate at seven of the nine lengths and tied at the other two. Overall the model got only 79 of the 900 problems right, so it is bad at long addition in both cases. What is surprising is that it does better on the harder kind. Method I generated 900 problems. For each length from 10 to 18 digits there are 50 pairs of random numbers whose sum stays the same length and 50 pairs whose sum gains a digit. The prompt contains only the two numbers and an equals sign, for example "4000000000 + 4000000000 =", and the model answers with its most likely output. An answer counts as correct if the last run of five or more digits in it equals the true sum. I also recorded the model's internal state on the last token of the prompt at every third layer. The states for the problems it gets right and the problems it gets wrong move apart as they pass through the network, and the gap is largest at layer 24 of 28. Limits - I did not count the digits in the model's wrong answers, so the length bias is inferred from the pattern in the accuracy and was not measured directly. Counting those digits would test whether the bias is real. - Each cell in the table is only 50 problems, so a difference of a few percentage points is one or two answers. - The internal states were measured on the prompt, before the model wrote anything. They show that the model treats the problems it will get right and wrong differently, but they do not show the bias itself. - I tested one model with one prompt format. The code, raw results and figures are public.

projects.title: Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness
projects.deepText: I found that the brightness of the white dwarf SDSS J112148.80+103934.2 rises and falls in a cycle of 117.4 minutes. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized remnant that is left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. The cycle appears in three separate sets of observations. The first is ground-based measurements from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), which is a sky-survey camera at Palomar Observatory. The second is five observing sectors of TESS, NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. The third is changes in the star's spectrum recorded by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). I also found a possible cycle of 3.431 days in a second white dwarf, WDJ215009.13+471257.26. Measurements in the survey images place the signal at this star and not at a neighbouring one, but the cycle still needs to be confirmed with another telescope. What is new and what is not - Both stars were already known, and what appears to be new is the measured cycles. - A search of catalogues and published papers, completed on 3 October 2026, found no earlier report of either period. This does not prove that nobody reported them first. - The first star was already known to be magnetic. The ATLAS survey had flagged it as a "dubious" variable and suggested periods that do not include 117.4 minutes, and that earlier flag deserves credit. - Neither result has been reviewed by an astronomer. This page is a public research record and not a peer-reviewed paper. - I have not established what causes the cycles. Rotation, a companion star and other explanations all remain open. Each dot is the average of the measurements at the same point in the cycle. The curve was fitted to the earlier nights only, and the later nights were not used to draw it. Method 1. I screened 400 nearby, faint, blue stars taken from SDSS and from Gaia, a satellite that measures the positions and distances of stars. 2. For each star I searched the earlier 75% of the ZTF observing nights for repeating cycles and saved the 20 strongest candidates. 3. I then tested those candidates on the later 25% of the nights without choosing any new periods, so a cycle found in the early nights had to predict the later ones. 4. For the 117.4-minute star I also checked the TESS observations and 96 SDSS spectra taken over 24 nights. A feature of the spectrum that was chosen from the first 16 nights predicted the final eight. 5. For the second star I fitted the star and its neighbours together in 359 ZTF images, to check which of them is the one that varies. Limits The image measurements for the second star reuse the same ZTF light, so they show which source varies but they do not confirm the cycle independently. The significance tests rest on assumptions about the noise that are not perfect. The follow-up with spectra also began after some of the spectra had been inspected, so it was not fully blind. What exists The analysis and the code were produced with OpenAI Codex under my direction. The repository holds the full record. One command downloads 123 MB of original observations, checks every file and recalculates the results from scratch, which takes about two minutes on my machine after the download. Rerunning it checks the calculation, and it does not replace a review by an astronomer.

projects.title: List to Cart
projects.deepText: List to Cart is a demo for quick-commerce apps, which are grocery apps that deliver in minutes. You upload a photo of your shopping list, and the app builds a cart from it. The list can be a WhatsApp screenshot, a list in a notes app or even a handwritten one. It works as a demo, and you can watch a video of it running on LinkedIn. How it works 1. You upload the image of your list. Claude 3.5 Sonnet then reads it and keeps only the names of the grocery items, so any other text in the image is left out. 2. For each item, the app shows several similar products. To find them, it turns the item name into a vector embedding, which is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of the text. It then compares this embedding with the embedding of each product's title, description and quantity, using Elasticsearch vector search. This kind of search is very quick, so it is suited to a real app. The words around an item name also count, which means that "Green Apple" or "Apple - 500gm" get different suggestions from plain "Apple". 3. You then pick products from the suggestions. The items on your list run down the screen, and the suggestions for each item run across it, so you can fill a cart very quickly. This speed matters in quick commerce, because delivery is so fast that slow cart-building is one of the biggest pain points. What production would need - A production version would need a smaller model to read the list in place of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and that model would probably be open-source. - Its recommendations would also need to take the user's own preferences into account, which my demo does not do. Why I built it I am forgetful, and I am usually asleep when my cook arrives in the morning. Because of this, I wanted to fill a cart and schedule a morning delivery for the cook to receive. No app offered that, so my wife and I kept our shopping list in a WhatsApp chat instead. That chat gave me the idea for a simpler flow, where I take a screenshot of the list, upload it and get a full cart straight away.

projects.title: Continuous Learning LLM
projects.deepText: This is a pipeline that lets a language model keep learning from its conversations with a user. It first decides which messages are worth remembering. It then condenses those messages into short insights, and finally it fine-tunes the model on them, which means training the model a little further on this new data. I tested it over 3 rounds of fine-tuning, and across those rounds the model recalled about 86% of the insights it was taught, while the best systems score between 90 and 95%. The model also lost less than 2% of its performance on the skills it already had. Automated fine-tuning is the low-hanging fruit, and I do not think it is the right answer in the medium or long term. It costs money, and a model cannot be fine-tuned forever, so it cannot learn from every single chat. The real problem is therefore picking the best insights from each conversation, and that is where I put most of my work. How it works Each message gets a priority score, which is built from five parts: - Novelty is 1 minus the highest cosine similarity between the message and the previous 500 messages. Cosine similarity measures how alike two texts are, so a message that is unlike all of them scores high. - Sentiment is scored from -5, which is extremely negative, to +5, which is extremely positive. - Excitement is scored from 0 to 1 and tracks how intensely the sentiment is felt. - Helpfulness is scored from 0 to 1 and tracks how useful the information will be later. - Centrality comes from a knowledge graph. A language model pulls subject-object pairs from the user's messages to build this graph, and messages that mention its central nodes score higher. Priority = 0.7 × novelty + 0.3 × excitement + 0.2 × centrality (normalised) + 0.1 × sentiment + 0.2 × helpfulness. Next, the messages are turned into a similarity graph. The Louvain method then splits this graph into clusters of messages that share a theme. I only understand Louvain at a working level, and it was o3 that suggested it. For the highest-priority clusters, which hold about 10 messages each, a model writes a 200-word synopsis. This synopsis is stored as a message as well, so that it also helps with retrieval later. Finally, a model writes a short question whose exact answer is that synopsis. These pairs of questions and answers become the data for fine-tuning. How I measured it - For insight recall, I asked questions about the new data after each fine-tune. Each question had one correct answer, and I counted how many the model got right. - For retention, I tested the model before and after fine-tuning on a private set of public questions, which are similar to the questions people ask chat models. Limits Each extra fine-tune raises the risk of catastrophic forgetting, which is when the model loses what it knew before. Because of this, the method needs changes before it can be used at scale.

projects.title: AI Agent Communication Protocol
projects.deepText: This is a protocol that lets a team of specialised AI agents pass work to each other. The team could include a research agent, a spec writer, a quality checker and a data analysis agent. The protocol is unfinished, because I have worked out the design and only partly built it. What it is The protocol is a message bus held in memory, which works like a group chat for the agents. I gave myself tight constraints for it: - It must run in a single process on my laptop, without any outside software such as Redis or Kafka. - Every message is logged permanently, so that anyone, such as a product manager, can replay a task and see exactly what happened. - It must work for language models, which means it has to handle everything from tiny prompts to very large files. How it works Every message is an envelope that cannot change once it has been sent. The envelope names the sender and the recipient, which can also be everyone. It also names a channel such as task, plan or result, along with some tags and the task that the message belongs to. - Each agent reads only the messages whose channels and tags it cares about. - An important message must be acknowledged by the agent that receives it. If it is not acknowledged, the bus sends it again, or the planner hands the task to another agent. - Large files such as PDFs or databases are not sent on the bus. Instead, the message carries a pointer to the place where they are stored. - Some steps can pause until a person or a QA agent approves the plan. - Secrets, such as passwords for a production system, never travel on the bus. A vault checks the agent's permissions and then hands the secret over directly. - A master planner picks the agent for each task using a score. The score is 0.6 × expertise + 0.3 × success rate over the last 30 days + 0.1 × a term that falls as the agent's queue of work grows. Status I designed the protocol and wrote its code with AI tools. It is still a work in progress, and I will write a full post about it when I have finished building it.

projects.title: Smart Medical Search
projects.deepText: Smart Medical Search lets you describe your symptoms in plain words, and it then suggests which kind of doctor you should see. It runs on a search index that links many kinds of medical terms to each other, such as diseases, symptoms, lab tests, medicines and doctor specialties. I built it in 2 days. It works well for matching symptoms to a medical specialty, but it still has two known problems, which are described further down this page. How it works The index is built with text embedding models. These models turn text into numbers that capture its meaning, so a query finds the terms whose meaning is closest to it. To search, you type a query and choose the category of terms you want back. The category I care about most is "Medical Specialty or Department", because the biggest use on doctor consultation apps is a person describing their symptoms so that the app can recommend a kind of doctor. For the query in this image, the top result is a gastroenterology specialist, which is the right answer. Known problems As of February 2025, neither of these problems has been fixed, although both look like simple fixes. - Mapping symptoms directly to diseases works poorly. This matters because it is a big use case. - The index holds many terms that are near-duplicates of each other. Because of this, the top 4 or 5 results are often the same answer repeated, and the query above shows this happening. Background At a previous company, before ChatGPT existed, I designed a way to build an index that links diseases to symptoms, lab tests, medicines, specialties and hospitals. The hard part was collecting the data, and our plan was to have several doctors supply it by hand over many hours. I left the company before the project started, and it never happened. When I mentioned it to a former colleague recently, I realised that text embedding models make this kind of index easy to build. Honestly, it is a shame that it took me this long to see that.

projects.title: AI Shoe Design
projects.deepText: AI Shoe Design is a web app that designs a shoe to match the existing look of a fashion brand. You upload photos of clothes and accessories that the brand already sells, and the app then generates a new shoe design in the same style. I built it quickly as a proof of concept for a former colleague. It is live and anyone can use it, and I would love to hear feedback on it. How it works 1. You upload up to 10 reference images from the brand's catalogue. You can try it with an example set of images from Zara. 2. OpenAI's o3 model then finds the design traits that the images share, such as their colour palette, textures, silhouettes and mood. It turns these traits into one detailed prompt for a single shoe that the brand could manufacture, and the prompt goes down to materials, heel height, colour codes and things to avoid. 3. You can read and edit that prompt. Writing the style out in words is the point of this step, because it gives the image model clear instructions and lets you change them easily. 4. Google's Imagen 4 Ultra model then generates the image of the shoe from the prompt. What makes it work The results are good because of the two models the app uses. The o3 model is very good at putting the shared style of a set of images into words. Imagen 4 Ultra impressed me even more, because it follows instructions well, avoids coherence errors and gives reliable results. Shoe design shows only a small part of what it can do.

projects.title: Grocery Crate Quality Check
projects.deepText: This demo checks whether a packed crate of produce is good enough for the customer who will receive it. You upload a photo of the crate and pick the customer's profile, which is either premium or average. The demo then answers "approved" or "not approved". It worked as a demo. It ran on free Hugging Face hosting, but that hosted copy is no longer online, so only the code is still public. How it worked 1. You uploaded a photo of a crate of any grocery item. The demo worked best when every item in the crate was of the same kind, although that could easily be changed for production. 2. You then chose the customer profile. The "premium" profile set a higher bar for quality than the "average" one. 3. When you pressed submit, the demo gave its answer. Crates were approved more often for average customers than for premium ones. Why I built it A quick-commerce company delivers groceries in minutes from small warehouses called dark stores. Such a company wants to send great produce to its best customers, while average produce may be fine for average customers. Managers can tell packers to keep this in mind, but packers may not always do it. An automated check would let the company spot-check packed orders, and this would make packers more careful about what they send to premium customers. How I would build it now I would not use a general AI model for this today. A check like this is a small yes-or-no decision, and there are now models and services made for exactly that kind of decision, such as Jev or a decisions API. I expect that one of those would do this job much better.

projects.title: Medium Articles on How AI Works
projects.deepText: These are four posts on Medium that explain in plain language how current AI works. Together they give anyone who is getting into AI a top-level understanding of large language models, the kind of model behind ChatGPT. The series is paused. I stopped writing while I was preparing for my wedding in the second half of 2024, and since then I have spent my time on hands-on AI work rather than on theory. The posts 1. AI Simplified: Machine Learning Basics. This is my favourite post, and it reduces neural networks to their most basic principles. It is probably also my best written post, because I had years to understand neural networks, whereas I learned about transformers much more recently. I highly recommend it to anyone who is getting into AI. 2. AI Explained: How to Teach an Old Computer New Words. This post gives a simple explanation of transformers, which are the T in ChatGPT. It uses examples from English and relates attention, the main idea in a transformer, to simple rules of grammar. It is heavily inspired by this 3Blue1Brown video, but it covers more ground and is simpler. 3. AI Explained: Objects as Vectors. This was the shortest and quickest post to write, and at first I thought of it as filler. Ironically, it is the most useful post for anyone doing knowledge work, because it teaches a way of thinking that applies to any field. 4. The Endgame of LLMs: Virtual Employees. This post sets out a plan for a true AI agent, and I wrote it in August 2024, before agents became popular. The plan and its techniques are now completely obsolete, because the field moved so fast that they were out of date about 15 days after I published them. The vision was big, however, and it still stands unconquered. I tried to build it and failed, and that is okay. The architecture from the fourth post for a general AI agent that can fill any role in an organisation. I made it with effort and love. Why I wrote them I love teaching, and writing these posts forced me to understand the material deeply. I also wanted a body of work that proved I understand AI.

projects.title: Parker Square Search
projects.deepText: This is my attempt at solving an unsolved maths problem, which is to find a 3x3 magic square made of nine different perfect squares. A magic square is a grid of numbers in which every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. I rewrote the problem with algebra so that the search code only has to loop over one number, and that code is public. It is a nerdy side project. I only gave it a few hours, and I do not plan to give it more. I have run the search on Google Colab for hours at a time, but the code has few optimisations, so it is just a shot in the dark. The problem Matt Parker made a Numberphile video about magic squares made of perfect squares. In it he showed a square that almost works but fails badly. That failed square is now called a "Parker Square", and the name has become a joke for maths that does not quite work. People have searched for a real one for years, and the search grew after the video came out, 8 years before I started this project. Nobody has found one yet, even though numbers up to 10^19 have been checked, and it is possible that one does not exist. A paper has proved that such squares exist for every grid size of 4x4 and larger, but the 3x3 case is still unsolved. How the search works A brute force search over nine separate numbers is futile. Working with o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.0 Pro, I therefore reduced the number of variables down to just one. - The nine numbers of the square can be written in terms of three variables, which are a, e and c. - Those three variables are then rewritten in terms of four more, which are X, Y, U and V, so that Y² − 2X² = D and V² − 2U² = D. - Both of these are Pell equations, which are a classic type of equation whose solutions can be generated by a standard algorithm. For any value of D, this algorithm gives infinitely many values of X, Y, U and V. - From X, Y, U and V I get a, e and c, and from those three I get all nine numbers of the square. This means that the search only has to step through values of D, and the conditions for a magic square are already built in. The README on GitHub has the full derivation. How you can help If you have a lot of spare computing power, please run the code. Optimisations to it are welcome and encouraged.

projects.title: Garden Watering System
projects.deepText: This is a gadget to automate the watering of my home garden. In it, an ESP32 reads a soil moisture sensor, and an ESP32 is a cheap microcontroller board with built-in Wi-Fi. The electronics sit in a weatherproof box in the planter. The sensing unit works and is installed. One problem is still open, which is that the battery power supply is not steady enough for a reliable long-term setup. How it works The ESP32 has a small processor, some memory and its own Wi-Fi, so it can run small programs and send data without a computer. It is programmed in the Arduino IDE. I had never used Arduino before and do not know its variant of C, so an AI model called o3-mini-high wrote all of the code. The soil moisture sensor connects to one of the analog pins on the ESP32. The moisture around the sensor changes its capacitance, and this in turn changes the reading that the sensor gives. When I put the sensor in a cap filled with water, its reading drops from about 3000 to about 2000. Build log - 22 January 2025: I tested the ESP32, and it connected to Wi-Fi. - 8 February 2025: I tested the soil moisture sensor. - 12 February 2025: I was waiting on parts. I had ordered an ESP32 expansion board to make wiring the project box easier, and I had also ordered a crimping tool and connectors, because my battery housing came without connectors. - 15 February 2025: I got the gadget working in the planter. The power problem The ESP32 needs a steady 3.3 V to run properly, but my two 1.5 V cells give only 3 V. This may make the system unstable. Because the ESP32 is used so little, I expect each set of batteries to last a few months. I will keep an eye on the battery, and if it does not hold up, I will add a DC-DC converter to give a steady voltage. Why I built it I am forgetful and have killed many plants. I watered them whenever I remembered, which always meant they got too much or too little water. I had also wanted to do an electronics project for years, especially one with an ESP32, because it is a magical and cheap board. So when my wife suggested automating the watering, I pounced on the idea.

projects.title: Claude with a Twitter Account
projects.deepText: I gave Claude 3.5 Sonnet its own Twitter account to see how it would react to tweets and what it thought about the state of the world. It posted a few tweets while it was running. In the end I abandoned the project, because doing it well needed a Twitter developer account, and that costs $200 a month. Destined to be lonely forever. How it works I wrote the integration with the Twitter API entirely from scratch. I then used GitHub Actions, which is GitHub's service for running jobs automatically, to trigger Claude's posts. Best of Claude on Twitter - What a beautiful statement - Not the reaction to Twitter humour you'd want - The only quote tweet it made What I learned I learned quite a bit from this project, including how to build a Twitter API integration from scratch and how to use GitHub Actions to trigger posts. I would have loved to keep going, but it cannot be done well without premium access to the API.
